records.source: וַיְהִ֣י כִשְׁמֹ֣עַ כָּֽל־הַמְּלָכִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ בְּעֵ֨בֶר הַיַּרְדֵּ֜ן בָּהָ֣ר וּבַשְּׁפֵלָ֗ה וּבְכֹל֙ ח֚וֹף הַיָּ֣ם הַגָּד֔וֹל אֶל־מ֖וּל הַלְּבָנ֑וֹן הַֽחִתִּי֙ וְהָ֣אֱמֹרִ֔י הַֽכְּנַעֲנִי֙ הַפְּרִזִּ֔י הַחִוִּ֖י וְהַיְבוּסִֽי׃
records.gloss: And it was, when heard all the kings who [were] across the Jordan, in the hill country and in the Shephelah and in all [the] coast of the sea the great toward [the] front of the Lebanon, the Hittite and the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite,
pieces: When all the kings west of the Jordan heard of this, the kings in the hill country, in the western foothills and all along the coast of the Great Sea as far as Lebanon, the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites,

L.1: And it came about, when all the kings who [were] across the Jordan heard [of it], in the hill country and in the Shephelah and along all the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites,

R.1: All the kings west of the Jordan River heard about what had happened. They ruled in the hill country, in the low hills to the west, and all along the coast of the Mediterranean Sea up to Lebanon. They were the kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites.

decisions.choice: heard: heard of Israel's victories
decisions.reason: The verb has no object. What the kings heard is what the Gibeonites hear in verse 3 and what the kings of the south hear in 10:1: Israel's taking of Jericho and Ai (chapters 6 and 8). The same opening, "when the kings heard", begins the next stories too (5:1; 10:1; 11:1).

decisions.choice: across the Jordan: here, west of it
decisions.reason: The phrase names the side of the river away from the speaker's starting point. In Deuteronomy, spoken east of the river, it means the west; here the book looks back from the crossing Israel has made, and the kings are those of Canaan proper, west of the Jordan. In verse 10 the same words mean the east, where Sihon and Og had ruled.

decisions.choice: the hill country, the Shephelah, the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon: the whole land west of the Jordan
decisions.reason: The three regions run from east to west: the central mountain ridge, the Shephelah ("lowland"), a belt of low hills between the mountains and the coastal plain, and the plain along the Great Sea, the Mediterranean, reaching north toward Lebanon. Together they name the whole of Canaan (compare 10:40; 11:16; Deuteronomy 1:7).

decisions.choice: Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites: the peoples of Canaan
decisions.reason: The list repeats the peoples God promised to drive out (3:10; Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1, where the Girgashites make a seventh). The Gibeonites of the following story belong to the Hivites (verse 7; 11:19).

decisions.choice: the western foothills (B); the low hills to the west (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the name Shephelah. Balanced and Readable say what it is, since the name is unfamiliar.

decisions.choice: the Mediterranean Sea
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "the Great Sea"; Readable uses the sea's modern name (m3).

decisions.choice: a sentence left open at the end of the verse
decisions.reason: The kings' gathering, the main clause, comes only in verse 2, so Literal and Balanced end this verse with a comma. Readable makes a sentence of each part.

records.heading: The kings join forces

records.source: וַיִּֽתְקַבְּצ֣וּ יַחְדָּ֔ו לְהִלָּחֵ֥ם עִם־יְהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ וְעִם־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל פֶּ֖ה אֶחָֽד׃פ
records.gloss: and they gathered themselves together to fight with Joshua and with Israel, [with] one mouth.
pieces: they joined forces to make war on Joshua and Israel with one purpose.

L.2: that they gathered themselves together to fight with Joshua and with Israel, [with] one mouth.

R.2: They came together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.

decisions.choice: with one mouth: in full agreement
decisions.reason: "One mouth" means that all speak alike, of one mind (1 Kings 22:13). Kings who were usually rivals agree on one thing: to fight Israel. The battle itself comes only in chapters 10 and 11, after the Gibeonites have gone the other way.

decisions.choice: with one purpose
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the idiom (m1); Literal keeps "one mouth", and Readable folds it into "as one".

records.source: וְיֹשְׁבֵ֨י גִבְע֜וֹן שָׁמְע֗וּ אֵת֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר עָשָׂ֧ה יְהוֹשֻׁ֛עַ לִֽירִיח֖וֹ וְלָעָֽי׃
records.gloss: And [the] inhabitants of Gibeon heard what had done Joshua to Jericho and to Ai,
pieces: But when the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai,

L.3: And the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,

R.3: But the people of the city of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai.

decisions.choice: Gibeon: a large town in the hills north of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Gibeon stood about six miles northwest of Jerusalem, at the site now called el-Jib, a hard night's march uphill from Israel's camp at Gilgal (10:9). It was a great city, "like one of the royal cities" (10:2), and later a town of the priests (21:17).

decisions.choice: and the inhabitants of Gibeon: set against the kings
decisions.reason: The sentence begins with its subject, not its verb, which in Hebrew narrative marks a contrast: the kings heard and gathered for war (verses 1-2), but Gibeon heard and chose another way.

decisions.choice: But
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "but" to show the contrast (m2); Literal keeps "and".

records.heading: The cunning of the Gibeonites

records.source: וַיַּעֲשׂ֤וּ גַם־הֵ֨מָּה֙ בְּעָרְמָ֔ה וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ וַיִּצְטַיָּ֑רוּ וַיִּקְח֞וּ שַׂקִּ֤ים בָּלִים֙ לַחֲמ֣וֹרֵיהֶ֔ם וְנֹאד֥וֹת יַ֨יִן֙ בָּלִ֔ים וּמְבֻקָּעִ֖ים וּמְצֹרָרִֽים׃
records.gloss: and they acted also they with cunning, and they went and made themselves envoys, and took sacks worn out for their donkeys, and skins of wine worn out and split and tied up,
pieces: they also turned to cunning. They set out posing as envoys, with worn-out sacks on their donkeys and old wineskins, cracked and tied up,

L.4: and they also acted with cunning, and went and made themselves out [to be] envoys; and they took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn out and split and tied up,

R.4: So they came up with a trick of their own. They pretended to be messengers sent from far away. They loaded their donkeys with worn-out sacks and with old wineskins that had split and been tied back together.

decisions.choice: they also: they too used a trick
decisions.reason: "They also" sets the Gibeonites beside someone else. It most likely points back to Joshua, who had taken Ai by a trick (8:2-8): the Gibeonites answer cunning with cunning. It may instead set them against the kings of verses 1-2, who chose open war.

decisions.choice: cunning: shrewdness, which can be good or bad
decisions.reason: The word is used of the prudence of the wise (Proverbs 1:4; 8:5) and of craftiness that deceives (Exodus 21:14). Here it is a plan to deceive, but the story also lets the Gibeonites be clever: by it they save their lives.

decisions.choice: made themselves out to be envoys
decisions.reason: The verb in the Masoretic Text is found only here; it seems to come from the word for an envoy or messenger (Proverbs 13:17), so the sense is that they disguised themselves as an embassy. A few Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient Greek, Latin and Syriac versions read a verb that differs by one letter, "they provided themselves with food", the verb used in verse 12. The Masoretic reading is kept; either way the next words describe the disguise. Reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: wineskins split and tied up: old skins mended for a long road
decisions.reason: Wine was carried in whole goatskins. A skin that cracked with age was mended by tying off or sewing the torn place. The Gibeonites show skins that look as if they had worn out on the way (verse 13).

decisions.choice: posing as envoys (B); pretended to be messengers sent from far away (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state plainly that the role was a disguise (m3). Readable adds "from far away", the point of the disguise (verse 6).

decisions.choice: So they came up with a trick of their own
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence and makes the link to what they had heard (verse 3) explicit with "so"; "of their own" keeps the sense of "also" (m1).

records.source: וּנְעָל֨וֹת בָּל֤וֹת וּמְטֻלָּאוֹת֙ בְּרַגְלֵיהֶ֔ם וּשְׂלָמ֥וֹת בָּל֖וֹת עֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וְכֹל֙ לֶ֣חֶם צֵידָ֔ם יָבֵ֖שׁ הָיָ֥ה נִקֻּדִֽים׃
records.gloss: and sandals worn out and patched on their feet, and garments worn out on them, and all [the] bread of their provision dry was, crumbs.
pieces: with old, patched sandals on their feet and worn-out clothes on their backs. All the bread they had brought for food was dry and crumbling.

L.5: and worn-out and patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out garments on them; and all the bread of their provisions was dry [and] crumbled.

R.5: They wore old sandals with patches on them, and worn-out clothes. All the bread they carried with them was dry and crumbling.

decisions.choice: crumbs: bread gone hard and crumbled, or spotted with mold
decisions.reason: The word appears again only in verse 12 and in 1 Kings 14:3, where it names some kind of small cakes or biscuits. It may come from a root meaning "spotted", which would describe bread speckled with mold, or it may mean bread dried and broken into crumbs. Either way, the bread looks many days old.

decisions.choice: worn sandals and clothes: the signs of a long journey
decisions.reason: Every item in verses 4-5 is chosen to look like the wear of weeks on the road. The detail matters because Moses had reminded Israel that in forty years their own clothes and sandals had not worn out (Deuteronomy 29:4).

records.source: וַיֵּלְכ֧וּ אֶל־יְהוֹשֻׁ֛עַ אֶל־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה הַגִּלְגָּ֑ל וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ אֵלָ֜יו וְאֶל־אִ֣ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵאֶ֤רֶץ רְחוֹקָה֙ בָּ֔אנוּ וְעַתָּ֖ה כִּרְתוּ־לָ֥נוּ בְרִֽית׃
records.gloss: And they went to Joshua, to the camp [at] the Gilgal, and they said to him and to [the] man of Israel, from a land distant we have come; and now, make for us a covenant.
pieces: So they came to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and told him and the men of Israel, "We have come from a far-off country. Now make a treaty with us."

L.6: And they went to Joshua, to the camp [at] Gilgal, and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant land; and now, make a covenant with us."

R.6: They went to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal. They told him and the men of Israel, "We have traveled here from a country far away. Please make a peace treaty with us."

decisions.choice: Gilgal: Israel's camp near Jericho
decisions.reason: Gilgal was Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, near Jericho (4:19-20; 5:9-10). It remains the base of the army in these chapters (10:6, 15).

decisions.choice: the man of Israel: the men of Israel as a body
decisions.reason: The word "man" is singular, used for the whole group of Israel's fighting men or their representatives (verse 7; 10:24). It is collective, not one person.

decisions.choice: a distant land ... make a covenant: the one kind of treaty the law allowed
decisions.reason: Israel was forbidden to make any covenant with the peoples of Canaan (Exodus 23:32; 34:12; Deuteronomy 7:2), but the law of war let Israel make peace with cities that were "very far from you" (Deuteronomy 20:10-15). The Gibeonites' first words are aimed at that rule: they claim to come from far away.

decisions.choice: covenant: a binding agreement between two peoples
decisions.reason: The word (berit) is the same one used for God's covenant with Israel. Between nations it is a sworn treaty that binds both sides, here with the Gibeonites as the lesser party (verses 8, 11).

decisions.choice: treaty (B); peace treaty (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "covenant". Between peoples the word means a treaty (m4), which Balanced and Readable say through the chapter; Readable adds "peace" so the purpose is clear (verse 15).

decisions.choice: Please
decisions.reason: Readable gives the Hebrew "and now", which turns to the request, as a polite "please"; Literal keeps "and now" and Balanced "so ... now".

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אִֽישׁ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־הַחִוִּ֑י אוּלַ֗י בְּקִרְבִּי֙ אַתָּ֣ה יוֹשֵׁ֔ב וְאֵ֖יךְ אֶֽכְרָת־לְךָ֥ בְרִֽית׃
records.gloss: And said [the] man of Israel to the Hivite, perhaps in my midst you [are] dwelling; and how will I make for you a covenant?
pieces: But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us. How then could we make a treaty with you?"

L.7: And the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you are living in my midst; and how shall I make a covenant with you?"

R.7: But the men of Israel said to these Hivites, "Maybe you live near us. Then how could we make a peace treaty with you?"

decisions.choice: he said ... will I make: the singular forms read in the margin
decisions.reason: The written consonants of the Masoretic Text have plural "they said" and a slightly different spelling of "I will make"; the marginal reading (qere), which the vowels follow, has singular "he said". The singular agrees with "the man of Israel" and "my midst", the people speaking as one. The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: the Hivites: the people of Gibeon
decisions.reason: The narrator now names the Gibeonites' people (verse 1; 11:19). The reader knows what Israel's men only suspect: these are Canaanites, among the peoples Israel was not to make a covenant with (Deuteronomy 7:1-2).

decisions.choice: in my midst ... will I make: Israel speaking as one
decisions.reason: The men of Israel speak in the singular, as one people, and address the visitors as one group ("you" singular). Their question rests on the law (verse 6 m3): if these people live in the land, a covenant with them is forbidden.

decisions.choice: us ... we
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the singular "my" and "I" of Israel speaking as one body (m3); Balanced and Readable say "us" and "we". Every level gives "men" for the collective "man", as in verse 6.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ אֶל־יְהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ עֲבָדֶ֣יךָ אֲנָ֑חְנוּ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֧ם יְהוֹשֻׁ֛עַ מִ֥י אַתֶּ֖ם וּמֵאַ֥יִן תָּבֹֽאוּ׃
records.gloss: And they said to Joshua, your servants [are] we. And said to them Joshua, who [are] you, and from where do you come?
pieces: They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." Joshua asked them, "Who are you? Where do you come from?"

L.8: And they said to Joshua, "We [are] your slaves." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you, and where do you come from?"

R.8: They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." Joshua asked them, "Who are you? Where are you from?"

decisions.choice: we are your servants: an offer to submit, said with courtesy
decisions.reason: The word (eved) is the word for a slave, a person who belongs to a master. Said by one people to another, "we are your servants" is the language of a weaker nation seeking a treaty under a stronger one (2 Kings 16:7). It is polite and humble, but it also offers real submission, which the end of the story turns into fact (verses 23, 27).

decisions.choice: who are you, and where do you come from: Joshua presses for names
decisions.reason: The visitors answered the question of verse 7 with a courtesy. Joshua asks directly who they are and from where; their answer (verses 9-13) names neither their people nor their town.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the hard sense with "slaves"; Balanced and Readable say "servants", as the style guide has it, since this is a polite formula (m1). In verse 23 the word becomes a sentence of real bondage, and there it stays "slaves".

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלָ֗יו מֵאֶ֨רֶץ רְחוֹקָ֤ה מְאֹד֙ בָּ֣אוּ עֲבָדֶ֔יךָ לְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ כִּֽי־שָׁמַ֣עְנוּ שָׁמְע֔וֹ וְאֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה בְּמִצְרָֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And they said to him, from a land distant very have come your servants, because of [the] name of Yahweh your God; for we have heard his report and all that he did in Egypt,
pieces: They answered, "Your servants have come from a very distant country because of the fame of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God. We have heard the reports about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and all that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did in Egypt,

L.9: And they said to him, "From a very distant land your slaves have come, because of the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God; for we have heard the report of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and all that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did in Egypt,

R.9: They answered, "Your servants have come from a country very far away. We came because we heard how great {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God is. We heard all about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and everything {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did in Egypt.

decisions.choice: the name of the LORD: his fame, what is known of him
decisions.reason: A name stands for the person and what is known about him. To come "because of the name" of the LORD is to come because his fame has spread (Exodus 9:16; 1 Kings 8:41-42, where a foreigner comes from a distant land for the same reason).

decisions.choice: what he did in Egypt and to Sihon and Og: old news, chosen with care
decisions.reason: The Gibeonites speak of the plagues and the exodus forty years earlier and of the victories east of the Jordan (verse 10). They say nothing of Jericho and Ai, the news that had moved them (verse 3): travelers from a far country could not yet have heard it. Their story fits their disguise, and yet, like Rahab (2:10), they do confess what the LORD has done.

decisions.choice: the fame of
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "the name"; Balanced gives its sense (m1).

decisions.choice: We came because we heard how great the LORD your God is
decisions.reason: Readable explains "because of the name" (m1) as a sentence of its own.

records.source: וְאֵ֣ת׀כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֗ה לִשְׁנֵי֙ מַלְכֵ֣י הָאֱמֹרִ֔י אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּעֵ֣בֶר הַיַּרְדֵּ֑ן לְסִיחוֹן֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ חֶשְׁבּ֔וֹן וּלְע֥וֹג מֶֽלֶךְ־הַבָּשָׁ֖ן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּעַשְׁתָּרֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: and all that he did to [the] two kings of the Amorite who [were] across the Jordan, to Sihon king of Heshbon and to Og king of the Bashan, who [was] in Ashtaroth.
pieces: and everything {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did to the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, whose city was Ashtaroth.

L.10: and all that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did to the two kings of the Amorites who [were] across the Jordan, to Sihon king of Heshbon and to Og king of Bashan, who [was] in Ashtaroth.

R.10: We also heard what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did to the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan River. They were Sihon, the king of Heshbon, and Og, the king of Bashan, who ruled from Ashtaroth.

decisions.choice: Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan
decisions.reason: Israel defeated both kings before crossing the Jordan and took their land (Numbers 21:21-35; Deuteronomy 2:26-3:11). Rahab names them too (2:10). Ashtaroth was Og's royal city in Bashan (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4).

decisions.choice: across the Jordan: here, east of it
decisions.reason: The speakers are now west of the river, at Gilgal, so the land across the Jordan is the east, where Sihon and Og ruled. In verse 1 the same words mean the west.

decisions.choice: east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "across"; Balanced and Readable name the side meant (m2).

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ אֵלֵ֡ינוּ זְֽקֵינֵינוּ֩ וְכָל־יֹשְׁבֵ֨י אַרְצֵ֜נוּ לֵאמֹ֗ר קְח֨וּ בְיֶדְכֶ֤ם צֵידָה֙ לַדֶּ֔רֶךְ וּלְכ֖וּ לִקְרָאתָ֑ם וַאֲמַרְתֶּ֤ם אֲלֵיהֶם֙ עַבְדֵיכֶ֣ם אֲנַ֔חְנוּ וְעַתָּ֖ה כִּרְתוּ־לָ֥נוּ בְרִֽית׃
records.gloss: And said to us our elders and all [the] inhabitants of our land, saying, take in your hand provision for the journey, and go to meet them, and you will say to them, your servants [are] we; and now, make for us a covenant.
pieces: So our elders and everyone who lives in our country told us, 'Take food with you for the journey. Go and meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Now make a treaty with us."'

L.11: And our elders and all the inhabitants of our land said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey, and go to meet them, and say to them, "We [are] your slaves; and now, make a covenant with us."'

R.11: Our elders and all the people of our country told us, 'Take food for the trip. Go and meet the Israelites. Tell them, "We are your servants. So please make a peace treaty with us."'

decisions.choice: our elders and all the inhabitants: a town ruled by its elders
decisions.reason: The Gibeonites speak of elders and people, not of a king. Gibeon is never said to have a king (contrast the kings of 10:1-5), and its decision is made by its leading men together with the townspeople.

decisions.choice: we are your servants: the words of verse 8
decisions.reason: The envoys report the very words they were told to say, and which they did say to Joshua (verses 6, 8). The whole mission was planned from the start.

decisions.choice: slaves (L); servants (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 8.

decisions.choice: meet the Israelites
decisions.reason: Readable names who "them" are.

records.source: זֶ֣ה׀לַחְמֵ֗נוּ חָ֞ם הִצְטַיַּ֤דְנוּ אֹתוֹ֙ מִבָּ֣תֵּ֔ינוּ בְּי֥וֹם צֵאתֵ֖נוּ לָלֶ֣כֶת אֲלֵיכֶ֑ם וְעַתָּה֙ הִנֵּ֣ה יָבֵ֔שׁ וְהָיָ֖ה נִקֻּדִֽים׃
records.gloss: This our bread, hot we took it as provision from our houses on [the] day of our going out to come to you; and now, look, it is dry and has become crumbs.
pieces: This bread of ours was still warm when we took it from our homes as food for the road, the day we set out to come to you. Look at it now: it is dry and crumbling.

L.12: This bread of ours, [it was] hot [when] we took it as provision from our houses on the day we went out to come to you; and now, look, it is dry and has become crumbs.

R.12: Look at our bread. It was still warm from the oven when we took it from our homes on the day we left to come to you. Now see how dry and crumbly it is.

decisions.choice: this bread of ours ... look: the envoys point to what they carry
decisions.reason: The speech becomes a display. "This" in verses 12-13 points to the bread, the skins, the clothes and the sandals the envoys hold up as proof of their story.

decisions.choice: crumbs: as in verse 5
decisions.reason: As in verse 5: hard and crumbled, or spotted with mold.

decisions.choice: warm from the oven
decisions.reason: Readable says why bread would be warm.

records.source: וְאֵ֨לֶּה נֹאד֤וֹת הַיַּ֨יִן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר מִלֵּ֣אנוּ חֲדָשִׁ֔ים וְהִנֵּ֖ה הִתְבַּקָּ֑עוּ וְאֵ֤לֶּה שַׂלְמוֹתֵ֨ינוּ֙ וּנְעָלֵ֔ינוּ בָּל֕וּ מֵרֹ֥ב הַדֶּ֖רֶךְ מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And these skins of the wine which we filled [were] new, and look, they have split; and these, our garments and our sandals, have worn out from [the] length of the journey, very.
pieces: These wineskins were new when we filled them, and see how they have cracked. And these clothes and sandals of ours have worn out on the long, long road."

L.13: And these wineskins that we filled [were] new, and look, they have split; and these garments of ours and our sandals have worn out from the very great length of the journey."

R.13: These wineskins were new when we filled them, but now they are split open. Our clothes and sandals are worn out because we have traveled so far."

decisions.choice: the very great length of the journey: the lie at the center of the story
decisions.reason: Everything the envoys show is meant to prove one claim: the distance. It is the claim the law turned on (verse 6 m3), and it is false: their towns were about three days away (verses 16-17).

decisions.choice: the long, long road
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts "very" last for stress; Balanced carries it by the repeated "long".

records.source: וַיִּקְח֥וּ הָֽאֲנָשִׁ֖ים מִצֵּידָ֑ם וְאֶת־פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה לֹ֥א שָׁאָֽלוּ׃
records.gloss: And took the men from their provision, and [the] mouth of Yahweh not they asked.
pieces: The men of Israel took some of their provisions, but they did not seek the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.14: And the men took some of their provisions, but they did not ask the mouth of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.14: The Israelite men took some of the travelers' food. But they did not ask {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} what to do.

decisions.choice: the men took some of their provisions: Israel's men examined or shared the food
alternatives: they ate with them to seal the treaty
decisions.reason: "The men" are the men of Israel of verses 6-7. Taking some of the visitors' food may mean they tested the bread to check the story, trusting their own eyes; or it may mean they ate with the visitors, since a shared meal could seal a covenant (Genesis 26:30; 31:54). The text does not say which; either way they judged by the evidence before them.

decisions.choice: they did not ask the mouth of the LORD: they did not seek God's answer
decisions.reason: To "ask the mouth" of the LORD is to ask what he says, to seek his decision. Joshua was to bring such questions to Eleazar the priest, who would ask of the LORD by the Urim (Numbers 27:21). The narrator states the failure plainly; it explains everything that follows.

decisions.choice: The men of Israel (B); The Israelite men (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose men are meant (m1); Literal keeps "the men".

decisions.choice: seek the word of (B); ask ... what to do (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the idiom "ask the mouth"; Balanced and Readable give its sense (m2).

records.source: וַיַּ֨עַשׂ לָהֶ֤ם יְהוֹשֻׁ֨עַ֙ שָׁל֔וֹם וַיִּכְרֹ֥ת לָהֶ֛ם בְּרִ֖ית לְחַיּוֹתָ֑ם וַיִּשָּׁבְע֣וּ לָהֶ֔ם נְשִׂיאֵ֖י הָעֵדָֽה׃
records.gloss: And made for them Joshua peace, and he made for them a covenant, to let them live; and swore to them [the] leaders of the congregation.
pieces: So Joshua made peace with them and made a treaty with them to spare their lives, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them.

L.15: And Joshua made peace with them, and made a covenant with them, to let them live; and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.

R.15: So Joshua made peace with them. He made a peace treaty with them that let them live. The leaders of the community also swore an oath to them.

decisions.choice: made peace with them ... to let them live: the terms of Deuteronomy 20
decisions.reason: The law of war set out how Israel was to deal with a far city that made peace: its people would live and serve Israel with forced labor (Deuteronomy 20:10-11, 15). Joshua grants the Gibeonites those very terms, on the basis of their claim to come from far away.

decisions.choice: the leaders of the congregation swore to them: the oath that binds Israel
decisions.reason: The leaders of the tribes (Numbers 1:16) swore in the name of the LORD (verses 18-19). An oath called on God as witness and judge, so it bound the whole people, and it could not be undone even when it proved to rest on a lie (verses 19-20).

decisions.choice: community
decisions.reason: Readable says "community" for "congregation", as in the terms for these books.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י מִקְצֵה֙ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֔ים אַחֲרֵ֕י אֲשֶׁר־כָּרְת֥וּ לָהֶ֖ם בְּרִ֑ית וַֽיִּשְׁמְע֗וּ כִּי־קְרֹבִ֥ים הֵם֙ אֵלָ֔יו וּבְקִרְבּ֖וֹ הֵ֥ם יֹשְׁבִֽים׃
records.gloss: And it was at [the] end of three days after that they had made for them a covenant, and they heard that near [were] they to him, and in his midst they [were] dwelling.
pieces: Three days after they had made the treaty with them, the Israelites heard that these people were their neighbors and were living among them.

L.16: And it came about at the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, that they heard that they [were] near to them, and [that] they [were] living in their midst.

R.16: Three days after making the peace treaty, the Israelites found out that these people were their neighbors. They lived close by.

decisions.choice: near to him ... in his midst: near to Israel
decisions.reason: The pronouns are singular, "him" and "his", referring to Israel as one people, as in verse 7. The Gibeonites lived close to Israel, in the land Israel was entering.

decisions.choice: at the end of three days: the truth comes out quickly
decisions.reason: Only three days pass. The time needed to reach the towns (verse 17) shows how short the "very long journey" of verse 13 really was.

decisions.choice: the Israelites
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject; the Hebrew says only "they".

records.source: וַיִּסְע֣וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַיָּבֹ֛אוּ אֶל־עָרֵיהֶ֖ם בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֑י וְעָרֵיהֶם֙ גִּבְע֣וֹן וְהַכְּפִירָ֔ה וּבְאֵר֖וֹת וְקִרְיַ֥ת יְעָרִֽים׃
records.gloss: And set out [the] sons of Israel and came to their cities on the day the third; and their cities [were] Gibeon and the Chephirah and Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim.
pieces: So the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} set out and came to their towns on the third day. Their towns were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim.

L.17: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel set out and came to their cities on the third day; and their cities [were] Gibeon and Chephirah and Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim.

R.17: So the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} set out and reached their towns on the third day. The towns were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim.

decisions.choice: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, Kiriath-jearim: four towns of one people
decisions.reason: The four towns lay close together in the hills northwest of Jerusalem, Gibeon the largest. Later they fell within the lands of Benjamin and Judah (18:25-28; 15:9, 60). Kiriath-jearim is where the ark stayed for many years (1 Samuel 7:1-2).

decisions.choice: on the third day: after a march of up to three days
decisions.reason: The town was reached on the third day after Israel set out, perhaps the same three days as verse 16. Either way the "distant land" was only a few days' walk from Gilgal.

decisions.choice: towns
decisions.reason: The word is "cities", which Literal keeps; Balanced and Readable say "towns", nearer to the size of these places.

records.source: וְלֹ֤א הִכּוּם֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כִּֽי־נִשְׁבְּע֤וּ לָהֶם֙ נְשִׂיאֵ֣י הָֽעֵדָ֔ה בַּֽיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּלֹּ֥נוּ כָל־הָעֵדָ֖ה עַל־הַנְּשִׂיאִֽים׃
records.gloss: And not struck them [the] sons of Israel, for had sworn to them [the] leaders of the congregation by Yahweh [the] God of Israel; and grumbled all the congregation against the leaders.
pieces: But the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did not strike them down, since the congregation's leaders had sworn to them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. And the entire congregation grumbled against them.

L.18: And the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel did not strike them, for the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. And all the congregation grumbled against the leaders.

R.18: But the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} did not attack them. The leaders of the community had sworn an oath to them in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. All the people complained against their leaders.

decisions.choice: sworn by the LORD the God of Israel: an oath in God's own name
decisions.reason: Israel was to swear by the LORD's name alone (Deuteronomy 6:13), and to break such an oath was to profane that name (Leviticus 19:12). That is why the leaders will not go back on it.

decisions.choice: grumbled: the word for Israel's complaining in the wilderness
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used when Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron (Exodus 16:2; Numbers 14:2). Here the people grumble against their own leaders, who had been deceived and who had acted without asking the LORD (verse 14).

decisions.choice: complained; all the people
decisions.reason: Readable says "complained" for the less common "grumbled", and "the people" for "the congregation", as the terms for these books allow.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ כָל־הַנְּשִׂיאִים֙ אֶל־כָּל־הָ֣עֵדָ֔ה אֲנַ֨חְנוּ֙ נִשְׁבַּ֣עְנוּ לָהֶ֔ם בַּֽיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְעַתָּ֕ה לֹ֥א נוּכַ֖ל לִנְגֹּ֥עַ בָּהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And said all the leaders to all the congregation, we, we have sworn to them by Yahweh [the] God of Israel, and now not we are able to touch them.
pieces: But all the leaders said to the whole congregation, "We swore an oath to them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, so now we may not touch them.

L.19: And all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them.

R.19: But all the leaders answered the people, "We swore an oath to them in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel. So now we cannot harm them.

decisions.choice: we, we have sworn: the leaders take the responsibility
decisions.reason: The pronoun "we" stands before a verb that already includes it, which puts weight on it: it was the leaders themselves who swore. They own the oath and its consequences.

decisions.choice: we cannot touch them: we are not free to harm them
decisions.reason: "Cannot" here is what the oath forbids, not what Israel lacks the strength to do. "Touch" means to harm, as in Genesis 26:11.

decisions.choice: may not
decisions.reason: Balanced says "may not" to show it is the oath that forbids it (m2).

records.source: זֹ֛את נַעֲשֶׂ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם וְהַחֲיֵ֣ה אוֹתָ֑ם וְלֹֽא־יִֽהְיֶ֤ה עָלֵ֨ינוּ֙ קֶ֔צֶף עַל־הַשְּׁבוּעָ֖ה אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁבַּ֥עְנוּ לָהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: This we will do to them, and let live them, and not will be on us wrath because of the oath which we swore to them.
pieces: This is what we will do with them: we will let them live, so that no wrath comes on us because of the oath we swore to them."

L.20: This we will do to them: we will let them live, so that there will not be wrath on us because of the oath that we swore to them."

R.20: Here is what we will do. We will let them live. Then God will not be angry with us for breaking the oath we made to them."

decisions.choice: wrath because of the oath: God's anger at a broken oath
decisions.reason: The wrath meant is the LORD's, who was witness to the oath (verse 19). Scripture tells of it later: when Saul killed Gibeonites, the land suffered a famine until the wrong was set right (2 Samuel 21:1-6).

decisions.choice: God will not be angry with us for breaking the oath
decisions.reason: Readable says whose anger is meant and that the danger was in breaking the oath (m1).

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֧וּ אֲלֵיהֶ֛ם הַנְּשִׂיאִ֖ים יִֽחְי֑וּ וַ֠יִּֽהְיוּ חֹטְבֵ֨י עֵצִ֤ים וְשֹֽׁאֲבֵי־מַ֨יִם֙ לְכָל־הָ֣עֵדָ֔ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר דִּבְּר֥וּ לָהֶ֖ם הַנְּשִׂיאִֽים׃
records.gloss: And said to them the leaders, let them live. And they were cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, as had spoken to them the leaders.
pieces: The leaders told them, "Let them live." So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation, as the leaders had said.

L.21: And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." And they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, as the leaders had spoken to them.

R.21: The leaders said, "Let them live." So the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole community, as the leaders had said.

decisions.choice: Let them live. And they became ...: the leaders' word, then the narrator's report
decisions.reason: The leaders' words are only "let them live". The next verb is the ordinary narrative form, so "they became woodcutters" is the narrator telling what came of it, ahead of Joshua's sentence in verses 23 and 27. Some ancient versions read it as part of the leaders' words ("let them live, and let them be woodcutters"); the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: cutters of wood and drawers of water: the lowest work of the camp
decisions.reason: Gathering firewood and hauling water were hard, daily, menial labor. Deuteronomy 29:10 names "the cutter of your wood and the drawer of your water" as the humblest members of the people, and these were jobs often done by outsiders. In Deuteronomy 20:11 a city that makes peace serves Israel with forced labor.

decisions.choice: as the leaders had spoken to them: as the leaders had decided
decisions.reason: "To them" may mean to the congregation, whom the leaders were answering (verse 19), or about the Gibeonites. Either way the arrangement was the leaders' decision.

decisions.choice: woodcutters and water carriers
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "cutters of wood and drawers of water"; Balanced and Readable use plain compound words for the same jobs, here and in verses 23 and 27.

decisions.choice: the Gibeonites
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are.

records.source: וַיִּקְרָ֤א לָהֶם֙ יְהוֹשֻׁ֔עַ וַיְדַבֵּ֥ר אֲלֵיהֶ֖ם לֵאמֹ֑ר לָמָּה֩ רִמִּיתֶ֨ם אֹתָ֜נוּ לֵאמֹ֗ר רְחוֹקִ֨ים אֲנַ֤חְנוּ מִכֶּם֙ מְאֹ֔ד וְאַתֶּ֖ם בְּקִרְבֵּ֥נוּ יֹשְׁבִֽים׃
records.gloss: And called for them Joshua, and he spoke to them, saying, why did you deceive us, saying, far [are] we from you very, and you in our midst [are] dwelling?
pieces: Then Joshua summoned them and said, "Why did you deceive us by telling us, 'We live very far away from you,' when in fact you live right among us?

L.22: And Joshua called for them and spoke to them, saying, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We [are] very far from you,' when you are living in our midst?

R.22: Joshua called the Gibeonites and asked them, "Why did you trick us? You told us, 'We live very far away from you.' But you live right here with us.

decisions.choice: deceive: mislead someone on purpose
decisions.reason: The verb is used of betrayal and trickery, as when Jacob says Laban deceived him (Genesis 29:25). Joshua names the trick for what it was.

decisions.choice: you are living in our midst: the lie set beside the truth
decisions.reason: Joshua sets their words, "we are very far", against the fact, using the words Israel had feared from the start (verse 7).

decisions.choice: three short sentences
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the question into a question and two statements; the meaning is the same.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֖ה אֲרוּרִ֣ים אַתֶּ֑ם וְלֹֽא־יִכָּרֵ֨ת מִכֶּ֜ם עֶ֗בֶד וְחֹטְבֵ֥י עֵצִ֛ים וְשֹֽׁאֲבֵי־מַ֖יִם לְבֵ֥ית אֱלֹהָֽי׃
records.gloss: And now, cursed [are] you, and not will be cut off from you [a] slave, and cutters of wood and drawers of water for [the] house of my God.
pieces: So now you are under a curse: you will never cease to be slaves, cutting wood and drawing water for the house of my God."

L.23: And now, you [are] cursed, and there shall never cease to be slaves from among you, both cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."

R.23: So now you are cursed. Some of you will always be slaves. You will cut wood and carry water for the house of my God."

decisions.choice: a slave will not be cut off from you: you will always supply slaves
decisions.reason: "Not to be cut off" means never to fail or come to an end (2 Samuel 3:29; 1 Kings 2:4). Among the Gibeonites there will always be those who serve as slaves; the bondage passes to later generations.

decisions.choice: cursed ... slave: the curse on Canaan
decisions.reason: The words recall Noah's curse on Canaan, "cursed be Canaan; a slave of slaves he shall be" (Genesis 9:25). The Gibeonites, a people of Canaan, receive that curse, but they keep their lives, which the oath had promised.

decisions.choice: the house of my God: the LORD's sanctuary
decisions.reason: There was no temple yet. "The house of God" here is the place of worship, where the tabernacle and altar stood (verse 27; 18:1). The Gibeonites' labor would supply the wood and water the sacrifices and washings needed.

decisions.choice: slaves at every level
decisions.reason: Here the word means real bondage, imposed as a curse and passed on (m1, m2). "Servant" would soften it into the polite "your servants" of verses 8-11, which this verse turns into fact, so every level says "slaves", as the style guide does where slavery itself is the point.

decisions.choice: Some of you will always be slaves
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the idiom (m1); Balanced keeps it closer to the Hebrew with "never cease".

records.source: וַיַּעֲנ֨וּ אֶת־יְהוֹשֻׁ֜עַ וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ כִּי֩ הֻגֵּ֨ד הֻגַּ֤ד לַעֲבָדֶ֨יךָ֙ אֵת֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֜ה יְהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֨יךָ֙ אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֣ה עַבְדּ֔וֹ לָתֵ֤ת לָכֶם֙ אֶת־כָּל־הָאָ֔רֶץ וּלְהַשְׁמִ֛יד אֶת־כָּל־יֹשְׁבֵ֥י הָאָ֖רֶץ מִפְּנֵיכֶ֑ם וַנִּירָ֨א מְאֹ֤ד לְנַפְשֹׁתֵ֨ינוּ֙ מִפְּנֵיכֶ֔ם וַֽנַּעֲשֵׂ֖ה אֶת־הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And they answered Joshua and said, for surely it was told to your servants that had commanded Yahweh your God Moses his servant to give to you all the land and to destroy all [the] inhabitants of the land from before you; and we feared very for our lives because of you, and we did this thing.
pieces: They answered Joshua, "Your servants were told for certain that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God had ordered Moses, {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servant, to give you the whole land and to wipe out all its people before you. So we were terrified for our lives because of you, and that is why we did this.

L.24: And they answered Joshua and said, "Because it was surely told to your slaves that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God had commanded Moses {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} slave to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you, we feared greatly for our lives because of you, and we did this thing.

R.24: They answered Joshua, "We were told what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} your God had commanded {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} servant Moses. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to give you all this land and to destroy everyone who lived in it. So we were very afraid that you would kill us. That is why we did this.

decisions.choice: the LORD commanded Moses to give you the land and destroy its inhabitants
decisions.reason: The Gibeonites have heard the very commands of Deuteronomy: the LORD would give Israel the land and Israel was to destroy its peoples and make no covenant with them (Deuteronomy 7:1-2; 20:16-17). They knew they were among those peoples, which is why they claimed to come from far away.

decisions.choice: it was surely told: the news was certain
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled, the Hebrew way of saying something was told for sure, not as rumor.

decisions.choice: we feared greatly for our lives: fear that led to cunning
decisions.reason: Like Rahab (2:9-11), the Gibeonites believe the LORD's word will come true. Rahab's fear led her to trust and to plead openly; theirs led to a lie, yet both were spared. The Gibeonites admit the deception without excuse.

decisions.choice: Moses his servant: Moses' title
decisions.reason: As in 1:1, the title marks Moses as the one who belonged to God and did his work.

decisions.choice: slaves / slave (L); servants / servant (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 8 for the Gibeonites and 1:1 for Moses. Readable has the Gibeonites say "we" for the formal "your servants".

decisions.choice: The LORD said
decisions.reason: Readable splits the long sentence and repeats the subject to begin the second part.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֖ה הִנְנ֣וּ בְיָדֶ֑ךָ כַּטּ֨וֹב וְכַיָּשָׁ֧ר בְּעֵינֶ֛יךָ לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת לָ֖נוּ עֲשֵֽׂה׃
records.gloss: And now, look, we [are] in your hand; as the good and as the right in your eyes to do to us, do.
pieces: Now look, we are in your hands. Treat us in whatever way you think good and right."

L.25: And now, look, we [are] in your hand; as [it is] good and as [it is] right in your eyes to do to us, do."

R.25: Now we are in your power. Do with us whatever you think is good and right."

decisions.choice: in your hand: under your power
decisions.reason: To be in someone's hand is to be under their control (Genesis 16:6). The Gibeonites give themselves up to Joshua's judgment, trusting the oath to protect their lives.

decisions.choice: in your power
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the picture of the hand; Readable gives its sense (m1).

records.source: וַיַּ֥עַשׂ לָהֶ֖ם כֵּ֑ן וַיַּצֵּ֥ל אוֹתָ֛ם מִיַּ֥ד בְּנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וְלֹ֥א הֲרָגֽוּם׃
records.gloss: And he did to them so, and he delivered them from [the] hand of [the] sons of Israel, and not they killed them.
pieces: So Joshua did this for them: he rescued them from the power of the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}}, so that they did not put them to death.

L.26: And he did so to them: he delivered them from the hand of the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel, and they did not kill them.

R.26: So Joshua protected them. He kept the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} from killing them.

decisions.choice: he did so: what follows, rescue and then service
decisions.reason: "So" points to what is told next: Joshua saved them from death (verse 26) and set them to work (verse 27). He acted as the oath required, against the people's wish (verse 18).

decisions.choice: Joshua
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject, Joshua.

decisions.choice: He kept the Israelites from killing them
decisions.reason: Readable joins the rescue and "they did not kill them" into one sentence with the same meaning.

records.source: וַיִּתְּנֵ֨ם יְהוֹשֻׁ֜עַ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא חֹטְבֵ֥י עֵצִ֛ים וְשֹׁ֥אֲבֵי מַ֖יִם לָֽעֵדָ֑ה וּלְמִזְבַּ֤ח יְהוָה֙ עַד־הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה אֶל־הַמָּק֖וֹם אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִבְחָֽר׃פ
records.gloss: And made them Joshua on the day the that cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for [the] altar of Yahweh, until the day the this, at the place which he will choose.
pieces: That day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and for the altar of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at the place {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would choose, and so they are to this day.

L.27: And Joshua made them on that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, until this day, at the place that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would choose.

R.27: That day Joshua made the Gibeonites woodcutters and water carriers for the community and for the altar of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. They would do this work at the place {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would choose. And they still do it today.

decisions.choice: the place that he would choose: the sanctuary God would choose
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy speaks again and again of "the place the LORD your God will choose" for his name and his altar (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11, 14). The Gibeonites were to serve the altar wherever the LORD set it, from the tabernacle (18:1) to the temple in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: until this day: the writer's own time
decisions.reason: The phrase looks from the time the book was written back to the events, and says the arrangement was still in force (as in 4:9; 7:26). Gibeon's people were still a distinct group in Israel in the time of Saul and David (2 Samuel 21:2).

decisions.choice: for the congregation and for the altar: the people's needs and the worship of God
decisions.reason: The work served both the camp and the sanctuary. Verse 21 spoke of the congregation; Joshua's curse (verse 23) named the house of God; here both are joined.

decisions.choice: and so they are to this day (B); And they still do it today (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Hebrew order, with "until this day" before "at the place". Balanced and Readable move it to the end, where it reads naturally.

decisions.choice: the Gibeonites
decisions.reason: Readable names who "them" are.
